utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, Madam Registrar, if you could kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam, and good afternoon to you. I see Mr. Josse is missing, otherwise I think we are more or less full house as far as counsel is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Prosecution, Mr. McCloskey is accompanied by Mr. Thayer. Interpretation is fine. I hear no complaints. Colonel, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome, and let's hope that we can get over with the last part of the cross-examinations, and then we'll see whether there is a re-examination by Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Sarapa, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, in connection with the last question I asked you yesterday, I wish to clarify something concerning the time of the events. In the transcript of 19th September, page 44, lines 1 to 3: [In English] " ... late May, early June, when leaving the compound in Potocari, we would face direct fire from vehicles shooting just in front or behind the vehicle."

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want --

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I just want to clarify something. Yesterday you said it happened in early July, not in May or June. Is it the same event?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we may simplify it. First of all, we're talking of the occasion that you were asked upon, namely when you are driving your vehicle and allegedly you were shot at and there were missiles falling in front and behind the car, which you were then asked about. Was there only one occasion when you were driving a car and you were fired at or more than one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This happened on several occasions, and it meant that I didn't have any driver anymore and Major Franken had to provide me with another driver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So at least we've clarified that. Now, Mr. Sarapa, you may direct the witness to the particular event that you had in mind, because I do recall that when you put it to him that it happened in June or July or May, he did not agree with that. So I suggest you go through this the best way you can. And I suggest the easiest would be to ask the

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: of May? And then in the month of June? You have already confirmed that in July you were certainly shot at. Mr. Sarapa, let him answer it because it will help you articulate your question better. Colonel, were you shot at while you were in your car in May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're talking about leaving the compound, then it happened indeed in June and July for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are excluding May, in other words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it might have been the end of May, beginning of June, but I can't quite remember anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you have a clearer picture than you had at the beginning of the sitting. So go ahead with your questions, Mr. Sarapa, I was only trying to help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it has been clarified. I just wanted to make sure whether we are talking about the same event. So it is the same event, late May or early June, when they were coming back from the base in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: You also mentioned later, line 10 and 11 that it was from a distance of about 50 metres from you and that it was very close. Do you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: Do you recall also being in a car and being shot at in the month
utterances.text: Yes. They were very close; I can remember that. And I can also remember at the moment when I drove away with my new driver, I had regular radio contact with the post and my previous major, who asked me if everything was okay and if I wasn't wounded. So I still remember that very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it has been cleared up. I would like to move on to another question. In your statement of the 28th September, 1995, you say: [In English] "One night on or around 8th of July I heard heavy shelling. The next morning personnel from the explosive disposal service went to see where they had landed. A few duds had landed about 500 metres from our compound. They were shells measuring about 2 metres -- measuring about 2 metres. I did not see this myself." [Interpretation] In this connection I would like to ask one question since you are an artillery officer. Do you believe it is possible for the shells concerned to have fallen because it was the so-called stray shell fired with certain original elements of aiming without the intent of targeting the base?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you understood the question, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've understood the question. There is always a possibility, but how big it was, that I can't answer, a question mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I should like to clarify only one point. I'm not talking about the size of the shell. I have already described from your words what the shell was like. The gist of my question is something else. Do you allow the possibility that it could have been a stray shell that was fired with initial aiming elements?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Can I interject here? Did only one shell land in the proximity of the car or more than one shell, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there are two things we are talking about and they're getting mixed up. When we talk about the shell that fell in the proximity of the compound, it happened when I was actually in the compound. I heard some shots that took place, so they are two separate, individual incidents that took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You were being asked about the incident of the 8th July. Allegedly you said in your testimony that: "One night on or about the 8th of July I heard shelling. The next morning personnel from the explosive disposal service went to see where they landed. A few had landed about 500 metres from our compound. They were shells measuring about 2 metres." My question is the following: As you're correct, there are two instances that are being referred to here. Let's start with the car incident, the car being shot at, was it only one shell or more than one shell that fell in the proximity of the car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was several times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And now the shelling in the proximity of the compound, was it one shell or more than one shell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I remember correctly, you heard shelling over the compound several times, at least one time that -- which was found in the proximity of the compound. Information as regards where the others landed I don't have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So now going back to Mr. Sarapa's question. Limiting yourself now to this one time where you found a shell in the proximity of the compound, would you exclude the possibility that this was a stray shell that happened to land there and that was not one which was intended to land there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I cannot exclude that. No, I cannot exclude that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So now you have it clear. I don't know if you want to pursue this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no need. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: My next question. This one I'm also asking you because you are a professional officer with long experience. In view of the situation in Srebrenica that you were very familiar with when you were there, namely that demilitarisation had not been carried out in full, that there were violations in terms of flights of helicopters and attacks of the division outside the enclave, do you believe the attack of the Drina Corps in July 1995 was an attack against the 28th Division or against the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: Do you recall also being in a car and being shot at in the month
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Very well. And my last question: After the termination of your mission in Srebrenica, did you face any limitations in divulging the facts concerning your mission?

utterances.speaker: Do you recall also being in a car and being shot at in the month
utterances.text: When I returned home to Germany, I was not allowed to divulge any information from the Ministry of Defence because it was to make sure that the troops in the area would still be safe. So that was a restriction. After that, later on, I didn't have any restriction anymore on divulging information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is more important, were you under such restriction or limitation when you released any of the interviews to the office of the -- to the investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was no longer applicable at that stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And are you under any restriction or limitation now for the purpose of your testimony in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not restricted. You could say that defence has withdrawn itself from it and have left it completely up to me. Right now in the preparation and during my stay here, I've had no escort and I haven't had any instructions from the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And for the purpose of your previous testimonies in other cases before this Tribunal, were you under any such limitation or restriction, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That covers the whole gambit of -- Mr. Sarapa, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions. You covered the last that I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And probably more quickly, too. So I thank you so much, Mr. Sarapa. Mr. McCloskey, is there a re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't have any questions for you either, Colonel. So that's it. We come to the conclusion of your testimony, and you can go back to your daily duties. On behalf of Judge O-Gon Kwon, from Korea, who is sitting to my right; Judge Kimberly Prost, from Canada, sitting my left; and Judge Bjorn Stole, from the Kingdom of Norway, sitting on my extreme right thank you for coming to give evidence in this case. Although we don't expect you going much too far from here, we wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, how long -- how much time do you think you require?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Two minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Usher, you can start preparing the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is a brief application concerning the Prosecution motion for the leave to amendment the 65 ter exhibit list which was filed on 13 September. The delay to respond to this motion is today on the 27th of September, and this is an application pursuant to Rule 126 to have an additional two days to respond to this motion. The reason I want this delay is because we had initially intended to file individual responses; now there is a way for us to file one response which would make it easier for the Trial Chamber to adjudicate on this motion. And no more than two days would be required for this purpose, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, any comments on your part?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No problem, Mr. President. I always appreciate being asked beforehand because I wouldn't have an objection, but no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Permission granted or an extension is being granted up to Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We still have to tender the exhibits. Let's start with the Prosecution. Thank you for reminding me, Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The first one is 65 ter number 0531. It's a message from Karremans to Mladic on the 11th and 12th of July. The next one is 65 ter number 1535, it's a photograph of the white house. The next one is 1992, it's a video-clip of the Hotel Fontana. And then 1993, another video-clip of the -- of the Dutch soldiers at the Hotel Fontana. 1994 is a video-clip of the second meeting at the Hotel Fontana. 1995 is the video-clip of the third meeting. And then 2037 is a video-clip showing the women and children and -- made -- at the time Major Boering coming out of the area of -- around Tiska Luka. And then 2047 is the -- now with the addition of the Hotel Fontana clips is the entirety of the trial video, as you recall from the other witness. 2048 is the transcript of the trial video, which includes some of the portions that we did not have subtitled. And then 2009, there was a short video-clip of the soldiers giving out candy. And then PIC00007 is map 6 from the map book that was marked briefly. PIC00008 is another section of map 6 that was marked by the witness. And then we have added P02105, which is a -- a chart or an index including a little more detail of the sources from the -- of the material from the trial video. I think you saw on the trial video there's a very brief source, but this is a little more in-depth for Your Honours. And that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Any objections from the Defence teams? I hear none. So all these exhibits -- all these documents are being so admitted. And Madam Registrar, you will assign the exhibit number later. Now we come to the Defence exhibits. We start with Defence for Popovic. There are three documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it's ID00019, ID -- 1D00019, 1D00020, and 1D00026. Any objections, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me one second, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want me to describe them to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've got them right here and I don't really think we have a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So these three documents are being so admitted and will be marked accordingly by the registrar. This is the Defence for Borovcanin, four documents. The first one is 4D00015, being a list of war criminals known to VRS who committed crimes in Bratunac, Vlasenica, Milici, and Skelani municipalities. Second one is 4D00025, which I understand is also a Popovic exhibit with the number 1D00018.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I'm being told that this was not told - - tendered, actually, by the Popovic, but it's marked by the Popovic team. The other document is the statement of facts and acceptance of responsibility by -- in the case of Momir Nikolic. And it's given 65 ter number 4D00016. And last an interim report of General Staff of AbiH submitted to the 1st Corps command signed by General Hasanovic. 65 ter 4D00017. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Mr. President, but just for your knowledge, the list of war criminals is a document that was found at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters and is incorporated in our later case. But coming in now is fine, no objection. And the statement of Momir Nikolic, as long as that's coming in in full, I have no objection. I don't think the whole thing was mentioned, but I think if it's going to be mentioned, it should come in in full. We saw a good part of it, I mean one whole page on the screen, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic or -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Since it was I who examined the previous witness, let me just give an explanation. At this stage we favour the proposal to introduce a part of the statement of Mr. Momir Nikolic, the part that we used in view of the standards you set at the beginning of the trial and since this statement I suppose will also be covered during the direct testimony of this witness, let me just say that we accept the exhibiting of the entire video recording suggested by the Prosecution number 52047, where we used the sequence from 7.42 until 9.10 for purposes of identification of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He's correct in that we -- as you know, Mr. Nikolic -- Mr. Momir Nikolic is on our witness list. We would at that time be submitting -- that's an important document, that -- it's a statement of facts pursuant to a plea agreement. I -- I have no objection of course it going in now, but I don't think we should see pieces of it. I think that might give the wrong impression. It's a very important document. It's coming in anyway, I would think, though I don't know if you want to go that far at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think that the best way to go about this is to admit the entire statement of facts and acceptance of responsibility for the time being, and then we see later, depending on whether the Prosecution eventually makes use or decides to make use of the entire document or not. But there's no point in having a piece -- a part of it which we would need to consider within the entire context of the statement itself. So -- otherwise, there are no objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you address -- do you wish to address the matters raised by Mr. Stojanovic or something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Just concerning the statement of the acceptance of responsibility that the Chamber just decided to admit, Mr. President, I believe it is important to know that this must be admitted on the record not for the truth of its content, but basically as simply a document that will be used with some witnesses. But I would object to the admission of - - that this document be admitted for the truth of its contents. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, I don't need -- we need any further positions on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would ask that it be provided -- that it be accepted for whatever value the Judges saw to it and we stay away from these old outdated common law --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll look at it as we go along and we'll decide what weight to give to it, if at all. So these are -- these four documents are all admitted. Now, I am going through what we have received. I noticed that although during your cross-examination, Mr. Meek, you did refer to documents you have not sought the admittance of any. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's correct. The documents I utilised were statements of the witness and just for showing him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just wanted to have a confirmation of that on the record. Same applies to you, Madam Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, the Prosecution has already exhibited the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. Now, Madam Faveau, you wish to tender nine documents. I'll go through them one by one. First one is 5D00040, which is a UNPF policy and information for the Security Council. Next is 5D00050, which is 2nd Corps ABiH structure UN document. Third is 5D00051, eight operation group structure UN document. Next is NIOD appendix 5, chapter 1, the conflict of the Medecins Sans Frontieres and the opstina, 5D00052. Again from the same publication NIOD, chapter 4, the emergency stock, 5D00053. Again from the same publication, part 3, chapter 4, section 9, the humanitarian situation in Srebrenica, 5D00054. Next is NIOD, the issue of people getting knocked down, 5D00055. Again NIOD part 3, chapter 6, section 16, the night of 10 to 11 July, last meeting between Karremans and the opstina, 5D00056. And last is a video number 44581/3, which is marked P1577. This hasn't been tendered already by you, Mr. McCloskey, this last video?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe we've agreed that that's going to be withdrawn because it has. I think Ms. Faveau was just worried about the time or the situation, but I think we've sorted that out.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. Yes, indeed, Mr. President. I confirm, it's the same video which the Prosecutor showed today, so video 2047, so there is no reason to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- okay. I'll be addressing the question of confidentiality and keeping some of these under seal for the reasons I will explain shortly, but do you have any objection to the admittance of any of these documents, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I would point out that the two BiH documents referred to are from the OTP collection, and as such I have no reason to question their authenticity. And Ms. Faveau did pay us the courtesy of showing us her intended exhibits, and we agreed that the NIOD -- the complete sections were fine to come in. And so we have no objection to any of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So the thing is that, as you will recall, while we were going through some of these NIOD documents, we needed to go into private session for the reasons that I explained then. I am not in a position now to distinguish -- to identify which one of these documents were the ones which we made use of in private session. So I am going to entrust the registrar with the task of identifying them, and those NIOD documents or parts thereof that were made use of in private session will be -- will be admitted confidentially and kept under -- under seal. All right. You will identify them because I -- here and now I don't remember which ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is a discussion here that perhaps there's no further need to have these under seal once the NIOD chapters that we have referred to are public domain now. One can read them on the internet, one can obtain a copy of them. What's your position, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that's correct, Mr. President. You know, the chances were that something could be gotten into, so I think it's safe to do it the way we did. But now I don't see any problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you agree, Madam Faveau, with lifting the precautions that we took earlier on?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we lift the qualification that we made earlier on now, and these -- all these documents will be entered -- entered into evidence, admitted into evidence, and marked according to the number the registrar will assign to them. Coming to Mr. Pandurevic's Defence, we have seven documents that the Defence wishes to tender. First one is 7D26, which is a request from the 28th Division to the Main Staff of ABiH. The second is 7D28, which is the 28th Division report to the 2nd Corps. The third is 7D30 which is BH army Main Staff response the Command of the 8th Operation Group Srebrenica. The next is 7D34 which is the 28th Division report to the 2nd Corps, which is 7D34. Next is 7D36 which is 2nd Corps order to the 28th Division. Next is 7D41, 2nd Corps instruction to the 28 Brigade. Last is 7D44 which is the Command of the 8th Operation Group Srebrenica with the operation and report. Now, the last was used in private session. What's your position on the admittance of these documents into evidence, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time, due to the small number of them, I will not object, though I do note that a few of these were used for a witness who didn't know anything about them. So they didn't really move us forward at all. Though they are relevant documents. And so at this point I won't object, but I think it's -- in the future, if that begins to continue, I think it -- I may be objecting because I don't think it's getting us anywhere. Though I would like to make sure that they are sent for translation so that we can see what they say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely the point that I wanted to raise. Almost none of them have been translated, and we need to have a translation. So they are being admitted, and of course we need to have them translated, otherwise they will be of no assistance to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would also point out as part of the -- their authentication, all of them but the 29 April 1995 document, 2nd Corps instruction to the 28th Brigade appear to be part of what we call the cobblestone collection, which I think, as you know, Mr. President, was captured by NATO forces after the -- after the war in the search of a Bosnian Serb army area. And it were -- these Muslim records were part of records that were kept by the VRS after the war. And so they have a particularly kind of unusual indicia of reliability to them. I'm not sure -- the other one is from one of the standard BiH collections, which I have no problem with the reliability with. But I think it's important for you to know that for that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So our decision is to admit these documents; however, those which have not yet been translated will be formally admitted only upon the translation having been done and made -- made available. Until then, they will only be marked for identification. Okay. But then automatically, once the translation arrives, registrar, you are already entrusted to finalise that. Mr. Krgovic, I take it that there are no documents that you wish to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we used just video-clip which is admitted earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any remarks before we bring in the witness? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Briefly, Mr. President, if I could be allowed to go give my respects to the witness. I'll be gone and back briefly, though I need to stay for one moment because Mr. Thayer will be addressing you on an interesting issue related to your recent ruling on adjudicated facts. This next witness -- I think we're attempting to save some time because this next witness has -- will testify about some of the adjudicated facts and we think we can reduce the questioning based on that. And Mr. Thayer will go over our ideas, which we've mentioned briefly to the Defence for your consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why don't you come in front and sit next to Mr. McCloskey because the positioning of the columns here are not to our liking.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We certainly read with great interest the decision last night, and I believe that we've been able to reduce certainly the questioning with respect to this witness by, as I counted, between 25 and 30 questions, which I hope will streamline the presentation somewhat. There are a few questions, though, Your Honour, which touch upon certain of the adjudicated facts but which may require some amplification. What we didn't want to do was give the impression that we were simply repeating facts that had clearly been addressed in the decision. We are quite mindful of the care that was taken with respect to the decision and will respect that. But there are necessarily certain areas we will need to repeat. One suggestion that we might have would be in certain circumstances to simply read the text of the facts of the witness, ask whether that is consistent with the witness's experience, and move on. That itself, we believe, might save three or four questions or a more extended answer. If that pleases the Court, we can certainly give that a try experimentally, at least at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness can sit down there. I thank you for that, Mr. Thayer. As you can imagine or you definitely would imagine, this is not something that occurs to you only; it's something that we have discussed and already decided upon, although you don't find it written down in the decision because it was not the kind of addendum that would have fitted in the -- and what I'm going to say applies equally to both Prosecution and Defence when it comes to the adjudicated facts. The witness can sit down for the time being. Basically, the decision means first that in as far as those 250- odd adjudicated facts that we have agreed with you upon, the Trial Chamber is simply taking judicial notice of the fact that that fact was adjudicated by a previous Trial Chamber. We are not going any further than that. The fact that a previous Trial Chamber has adjudicated that on the 11th of July, 1995, the VRS entered into Srebrenica does not mean that the chapter begins there and finishes there, and that you are -- neither you nor the Defence are entitled to expand on that. There are some adjudicated facts that obviously go in favour of your case and there are several adjudicated facts that go in favour of the Defence case. What we have stated there is what I have told you, and if you need to expand on that to make things clear - because ultimately it's we who will have to adjudicate not only on that fact but all the facts that are pertinent - of course you will be able. But you will not be expected to elicit answers from a witness simply to repeat what another Chamber has already acknowledged, and that -- what we have already accepted as being an adjudicated fact by another Trial Chamber. I don't know if I have made myself clear enough. It's meant, of course, to accelerate the process and we have steered away from what we considered would have constituted a prejudice to a fair trial -- to the fair trial of the accused. But again within the limits set. The other thing is this, it seems you have taken a decision. In our mind we must go a step further than you and remind you that the decision, both one and the other, are still subject to possibly -- I'm just using the term -- word "possibly" being -- becoming the subject matter of an appeal, so do keep that in mind. But for the time being, you know what our rules are. The decisions that we handed down yesterday have carried their legal consequences as from the moment they were handed down, and that's it. But do keep also in mind that things may change, in which case, of course, the question will arise whether you would require a witness to come back so that he or she answers questions that you wouldn't have put because of our two decisions. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification and guidance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I may have a moment just to take the podium and gather my things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, it appears that I've missed the witness, so I'll be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Van Duijn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you kindly stand up. Are you still in the Dutch armed forces? Are you still a member of the Dutch armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm currently working for the Dutch Royal Marechaussee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And do you have a rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a major.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're a major. So if we address you as Major Van Duijn --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- would that suit you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So. Thank you, Major, and welcome to this Tribunal. You have already testified in Krstic and Blagojevic trials, so you more or less know the procedure. I won't dwell on that. Madam Registrar is going to hand to you a copy -- the text of the solemn declaration that our rules require every witness to make before he or she starts giving evidence. Please read it out loud and that will be your undertaking with us that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Major. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We will be speaking the same language. Nevertheless, there will be translation into a couple of other languages. So I'm going to try to speak slowly and I ask that you perhaps speak a little more slowly than ordinary and please leave a pause between the end of my question and the beginning of your answer or the beginning of anybody else's question and your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And before you ask the first question, could I kindly ask the entire staff, that's you, technicians, recorders, interpreters, whatever, up to what time beyond quarter to 4.00 can we go before we have a 30-minute break? I'm suggesting it is possible to -- the break will be at quarter to 4.00 normally. If we go till quarter past -- no, that will not. No, I think we have to work it out in a different manner. Let me ask the registrar to work it out, and she will communicate with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Sorry for that, Mr. Thayer, but, you know, we need to be elsewhere in this Tribunal at 5.00 for a short while, and then we will re-convene.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, will you please state and spell your name.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: My name is Leen Van Duijn spelled L-e-e-n V-a-n D-u-i-j-n.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how old are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I am 36 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You are currently a major in the Royal Dutch army?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Presently serving in Italy with the European Gendarmarie force?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just briefly would you let the Trial Chamber know what that is and what you do there.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Just a specification, I'm not working in the army, but in the Royal Marechaussee which is similar to the army but a different unit. I'm working for the European Gendarmarie force, which is a new unit, and I'm working in the headquarters based in Vicenza, Italy. It is a new police force, robust police force which has been set up by five nations from -- which are also Member State from the European Union namely France, Italy, Spain, Portugal, and the Netherlands, and we are capable of doing all sort of police missions all around the world. And at that headquarters in Vicenza, I'm in the head of training, evaluation, and lessons learned department.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me just review briefly your military service. You were commissioned into the army as a second lieutenant. Upon graduating from the royal Dutch military academy in 1993. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you were promoted to first lieutenant in November 1994, then deployed soon thereafter in Bosnia as a platoon commander from January of 1995 through July of that same year. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And then between the latter part of 1995 and 1999, you served as a platoon commander in the air mobile brigade training battalion and later as a special reconnaissance platoon commander. Is that correct as well?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in 1999, you were promoted to captain while serving as an intelligence officer. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Between 2000 and 2005, you were based at Schiphol airport where you were promoted to major and eventually headed the criminal investigations division at the airport. Is that correct as well, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The break will be as planned beforehand at 3.45.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And since then you've been with the European Gendarmarie force. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention to the time of your actual deployment to Bosnia and ask you to please describe the process you underwent as you first entered the enclave in January of 1995.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: In the beginning of January we -- we entered by route from Zagreb with bus to the enclave, and at every single crossing or check-point we were asked to get out of the bus, show our ID cards, everything was checked, our luggage was searched. And basically we were -- every time everything was turned inside-out before we could enter eventually the enclave. And everything that was not allowed by the Serb forces was taken out of the luggage, which was basically everything they wanted to take from us, meaning drinks or smoking materials or everything they wanted to take out of it, it was possible for them to take out because we were unarmed and travelling to -- by bus to the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you just stated that you were unarmed. Were you unarmed by choice or was that a condition that was imposed on you by someone?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That was imposed and was brought to us as the regulations that were standard at that time. So we didn't choose for it but it was imposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And whose regulations, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I heard from my higher level that that was the way that we should conduct things, and I don't know at what level that was agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was that a United Nations or UNPROFOR decision or a decision that was made by someone else?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Very well. When you entered on duty, can you describe for the Trial Chamber, what were your duties and responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I was the head of an area which was -- which kept the observation post Romeo and Quebec and with my platoon we had to patrol that area and man the two observation posts to guard the outskirts of the -- of the enclave on the north-eastern part, the total north-eastern part of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were there any particular OPs that -- that you manned or that you were responsible for, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That were OP Romeo and Quebec.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you assigned to a particular company?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: My company was the Charlie company which was located in the northern part together with the staff of the battalion positioned on the base at Potocari, and the other company, Bravo Company, was situated in Srebrenica town and manned the southern part of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, before focussing on some of your experiences in July of 1995, I'd like to turn your attention to some other particular aspects of your service in Bosnia. Specifically with respect to the re-supply of the DutchBat forces in the enclave. In general, sir, can you describe the frequency of the re-supply that -- that the DutchBat forces received while you were there?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: There was no clear frequency, at least there were a lot of re- supply convoys scheduled, but a lot of them were stopped by the Serb forces because they did not get a clearance to get through to -- to us. When I arrived in January there was already a problem which occurred regularly with the fuel situation, and next to that we had problems managing the small amount of food and making sure that we had enough drinking water because we also needed fuel to run the modules to make drinking water out of the water that was present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me just stop you right there. At some point, sir, did the -- the frequency or the scheduling of the re-supply convoys change in some fashion?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Basically the scheduling was the same, only from March/April on, the poor conditions that we had became even worse because from that moment on a lot of the -- even more of the convoys were cancelled because they did not get clearance from the Serb forces. Next to the re-supplying, also personnel from DutchBat that went on leave were not allowed to return to -- to the enclave. So the situation tightened. Less convoys came through, and we had more problems, personnel and material-wise.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were a platoon commander. Is that correct? I want to ask you how the restrictions on the re-supply affected your operability on the ground, that is, how did it affect your ability to do your job?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Well, of course the personnel situation was of a sort that if you don't have enough food or drinking water, your health situation diminishes and there were a lot of people from DutchBat that had problems with their health, stomach problems or otherwise, weakened. Next to that, the operational -- the observation posts tried to change -- tried to -- tried to trade with the local population to give them coffee and we would receive bread in order to keep that -- keep that in a better shape, to keep themselves in a better shape. For me as the platoon commander stationed in Potocari and in charge of re-supplying the observation posts, it meant that we -- because of the lack of fuel, we had to do that, re-supplying by foot, four- or five-hour patrol, using horses from the local population, to carry food packets up to the observation post that were situated on the hilltops. Because there was not enough fuel to do our patrolling with the vehicles we had, so this also meant for the operational side that we had less information of the area and were less frequently present because the patrols were only manageable on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just going back to something you mentioned a few moments ago, sir. You mentioned some of the soldiers having stomach problems. What were they eating?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: We only ate rations. Basically, the last four months of the -- of the tour every day, which meant that there were so much preservatories present in that canned food that they had stomach problems every time they ate something or drank something.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, would you describe for the Trial Chamber, sir, the effect, if any, on the restrictions on your weapons systems, your individual weapons and your ammunition as well, please.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: When it came to our individual weapons, we had no possibility to train with them, but also the state in which they were, they were already a few years there. It was a poor state. Next to that, the ammunition we had for our personal fire-arms were in such a state that sometimes even the bullets fell out of the casings because they were too old to be used. And when it comes to rocket-launchers or bigger ammunition, the indicators for the humidity were so far out of the -- so far out in the red that it was dangerous to shoot them, to use them, because of the possibility they would explode in -- in the hands of the person that wanted to fire them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And were you able to repair any of these weapons, whether it's the rocket-launchers or your personal weapons?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: No. We had limited means to repair, and when weapons are in such a state, there's no repairing them. You just have to have new weapons or new ammunition, which was not possible because of the convoys being refused and not having clearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how about spare parts for the weapons, were there any restrictions on spare parts coming into the enclave by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The spare parts were treated the same, more or less as the other convoys. So also those spare parts or new weapons were refused to be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to turn your attention now to July of 1995 and ask whether you recall the VRS attack on the enclave?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when that attack began?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The attack started at the 6th of July when the first rockets came flying overhead and the first bombings started. We had to go to the bunker when I was at the -- at the base at Potocari at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you actually observe shells in the air?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I actually saw rockets flying overhead, coming from the direction of the north part and aimed at the -- at the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And could you describe the intensity of the shelling, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: It was very intense, constant shelling of the whole area, and to give an idea that from January on it was the task of the platoons and the observation posts to count the number of shootings and detonations that we heard or saw in the enclave. But from the 6th of July, we basically stopped because there was no counting the number because it was constant and very intense.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you recall approximately how many days the shelling lasted?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Basically from that day until the day that the Serb forces entered the enclave and took over, so that's the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention now to the 9th of July, Major, and ask you whether you received an order at that time to take up a certain position.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: On the 9th I got the assignment to go with the rest of my platoon because two of my groups were already positioned on the OPs Romeo and Quebec, but with the rest of my platoon and with the quick-reaction force to go and help the Bravo Company setting up the blocking positions south of Srebrenica town in order to stop the advancing of the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall approximately what time and what date you established those blocking positions, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I think it was the end of the 9th when I got the -- the assignment, and during the night I want over to Bravo Company and Captain Groen briefed me on the situation and gave me the mission to take in Bravo 3 location. And so during that night in the early morning of the 10th, I was present at that -- at that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you describe for the Trial Chamber, please, where that blocking position was actually located.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: It was in the southern part of Srebrenica town on a road that went from Srebrenica town to a former town called Crni Guber, if I pronounce it correctly, and it was on a road looking south -- south of the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And from that position were you able to observe the town of Srebrenica, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes. To the north I saw the town of Srebrenica, and to the south I saw the hills south of the town. But I was able to look both ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that it is 3.45, so we'll take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. We'll have a break until 4 -- ten minutes past 4.00, ten minutes past 4.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So now we'll go till 5.00. We'll have a break at 5.00, and then we will resume at 5.30. And from 5.30 right through 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Major, when we broke you were describing your blocking position just south of Srebrenica town. Were you able to observe the shelling of the town from that blocking position?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes, I was. Shelling was on our location, but also on the town. And it changed every half-hour, 45 minutes, they would shell on the town. We could see the shelling --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Major, one moment. We're having some technical issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you follow the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to re-connect basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do we have lift-off, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, I think we have got everything here. Let me check that the pages and lines tally. Yes, you can go ahead, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Major, you were just describing the shelling that you both observed and experienced from your blocking position. Would you please continue.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: We could see the shelling coming down on the town of Srebrenica, and as I said, every 30, 45 minutes it would change. It would go quiet for five to ten minutes, and then the shelling would start at our -- our own location. And then we would have that again for the same period of time, and then it would change again to shell the town. And we could see it from -- I could see it from my location, shelling, hitting houses, and houses exploding or -- after that, the detonations and smoke coming from houses from that detonations and shellings.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you described shelling of your position. Can you describe for the Trial Chamber, please, the proximity with which the shells were striking near your position.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Shells fell down approximately between 50 and 100 metres from my APC, even so dirt coming from that -- from the impacts fell on our APCs, so very close by my location.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you later adjust your blocking position, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes. Later on we withdrew a little back towards an intersection basically more towards the other APCs that were also standing in the blocking position.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was this at a particular location within Srebrenica town, sir, to which you drew back?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: It was a closer-by, a crossroads, and close to an area which contained also the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, during this time did you have an opportunity to observe the inhabitants of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes. At first, even during the night, we could see a lot of people fleeing from the south or coming from the south with everything they could carry and going to the northern part of the enclave. We could see a lot of civilians that were very scared and frightened, of course, and they would cross our position and go and follow the road to the north. Next to the civilians, we also saw of course the Muslim soldiers that at first stayed on our location, and later on also went up to the north. And then finally, we were there alone, standing there alone, in a desolated part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So where did you spend the night of 10 July, Major?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I spent it in the APC doing cat-naps, more or less staying in close contact with the other APCs and the rest of my personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So that brings us to the morning of 11 July. Major, can you describe the scene in Srebrenica at that time?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: When I came from -- because that was basically the period when we were drawing back through the town because the whole area, the southern area of Srebrenica was empty, no one was there. All the refugees were gone and also the Muslim soldiers were -- were gone. So that gave us the opportunity to retreat and get in closer contact with the -- the civilians that had gathered at the compound of Bravo Company in Srebrenica town itself. When we came there, it was one big chaos where people were very scared and hysterical and running through each other and grabbing whatever they could take with them and running or walking to the north, following the road. It was, in one word, a chaos.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So what did you and your men do, Major, from there?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: At that time, my mission was to withdraw to the compound of Bravo Company in order to take up position there so they could leave there and withdraw to Potocari. And my mission was to stay there and to make more or less other blocking positions to give them time to retreat and to give all the refugees time to make their way to the north to the area of Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you described the chaos and the refugees moving north. Were they assisted in any fashion by other members of DutchBat in that move to the north, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes, we tried in any way to help them by getting refugees that were not able to walk or go north by themselves, getting them on vehicles, on trucks, or even on our own APCs, aiding refugees while helping. So we had soldiers walking with the refugees to -- to the north, and basically we tried to help them in any way we could at that time, which was helping them getting away from that place to the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you describe the positioning of you and your men in relation to this mass of people that were moving north to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: At first we were standing next to the compound of Bravo Company in the middle of chaotic circumstances with a lot of refugees, but the refugees were leaving and at the stage that everything was empty, so every refugee had left that location. We took up another position more to the north, in order so that we could see basically the -- the back of the caravan of refugees going to the north, and we would have a few hundred metres from them and taking up blocking positions every time. If we lost sight of them, we would move north again to take up another blocking position, in order to safe-guard the retreat of all the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you please, Major, describe for the Trial Chamber what would happen as you proceeded north, taking those blocking positions one at a time?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Basically when we took up our position we were staying there until of course all the refugees were -- were gone and had the possibility to go to the north. The people that were not able to walk or had other problems, we would take in or on top of our APC. And we would stay in that location as long as possible. Basically that meant until the shelling near to our location started again. We could see that the shelling came closer to our location, and that was for us a sign to retreat another few hundred metres again and take up position until the shelling on that position would start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And physically, where were the shells falling in relation to your position, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Basically we could see that the shelling would start in a normal way shelling is conducted. So a few shells would fall further from our location, sometimes even behind our position. Then the shells would fall in front of our position, and then that was, for us, the sign to leave because the next shells would hit in the direct vicinity of our position. That is a normal procedure when you conduct artillery fire, so that is basically the course of events that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what kinds of weapons did you have available to you in your APC?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Next to the white UN APC that was clearly visible, we only had a heavy machine-gun mounted on top. We had our personal fire-arms, and we had some rocket-launchers that, as I mentioned before, had the humidity indicators well in the red area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall where you spent the night of 11 July, Major?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The night of the 11th, I took up a position near the point 02, a location as we know as 0.02, and we positioned four APCs, two on each side of the road, and we spent the night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you describe where this 0.02 location is in respect to the main compound in Potocari, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: It is just south of the main compound, and it must have been 1 or 2 kilometres south of the entrance of the compound, in which you have an intersection, a road leading to, as we know, OP Mike, and a town of Susnjari.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: While you were waiting at 0.02, Major, or while you were posted there, were you waiting for anyone in particular?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: At first we took up the position at 0.02. Just a few hours later we took up a position of just north of 0.02 because the shelling at 0.02 was also too heavy to with stand. So we took up a position just north of that, a location, but we also had to wait for Sergeant Mulder, the commander of the OP Mike, which had radioed in and said that he would come with his APC and escorting a caravan of refugees from the area of Susnjari. And they would be walking alongside the APC and on top of the APC and coming to the camp in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did Mulder and the refugees in fact arrive, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes. Late in the evening they arrived. It must have been around somewhere 11.00, 12.00 at night, and I had a conversation with Sergeant Mulder, as my personnel helped getting all the refugees off the APC. And just to give an estimation of the amount of refugees, it took us about 45 minutes to get all the refugees off the APC because they were all seated on top of the APC. And the rest of the people that were walking alongside the APC went through to the other refugees that were situated on the -- on the areas just south of the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, at this position a bit north of 0.02, did you also see any Muslim men at that time?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: In fact, that was still when we were located at 0.02, we saw a big group of men going towards Susnjari, so leaving from 0.02 towards OP Mike, so the other direction, and we could see them leaving -- carrying small-calibre weapons with them. Men of all sorts of age, even young boys and old men with them. Not all of them were armed, but they were all men and going in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you see anyone you recognised, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I recognised a small boy of about 11 or 12 years old. I don't recall his name, but he was living in a town near to OP Quebec, and he even helped my platoon members in getting water for the OP and stuff like that. So we -- I knew him from -- from his face and also from his name, and he was also in that caravan.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So that brings us now to the morning of 12 July, Major. Were you still posted at that location just to the north of 0.02?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you receive any briefing at that time concerning the status of the other OPs?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: At 6.00 in the morning I heard over the radio that my last OP, OP Quebec, because OP Romeo was already gone, that OP Quebec also was no longer there and the personnel was taken by the Serb soldiers away from that location and basically there were no more present there at OP Quebec.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Major, did you at some point that morning also receive information that Bosnian Serb forces had in fact been sighted on or near the UN compound in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes. Later that morning basically the message was that Bosnian Serb soldiers had taken over -- the Bosnian Serb forces had taken over the enclave, and they were also sighted near the UN compound in Potocari and -- which led to the assignment for us to put away our weapons, to raise our heavy machine-gun which was mounted on the APCs to the skies. We had to put all our personal weapons in one APC, which was my APC. And basically what was left for us then - and that was also the assignment I got - that we from that moment on only could give humanitarian aid, because the Serb forces had taken over the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, did you yourself subsequently see VRS soldiers; and if so, can you describe for the Trial Chamber from what direction they were coming and in what direction they were headed, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The first Serb soldiers I saw were soldiers that were moving through the fields east of my location, and they would come up the road at 0.02. And after some of those forces had searched the houses in the vicinity of 0.02, they came up walking north to -- to my location. And other Serb forces were coming from the north and also the -- through the radio we could hear that Serb forces crossed the -- the OP Papa that was north -- the most northern check-point at the road, and they were moving south. So basically at the same time Serb forces came up from the south to the north, from OP -- from 0.02, and from the north to the south at my location.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what can you recall about the clothing or uniforms, insignia and so forth, that these Serb soldiers were wearing?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Basically the clothing was of a military type, but it was a mixture of all sorts of personal items with bandannas and with all sorts of colours mixed with camouflage pattern clothing. And I recall one of that soldiers having Serb flag draped around his soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So your weapons are locked away, your gun is up, and you're seeing the soldiers arrive. What did you do next, Major?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: After the initial stage which we saw Serb soldiers handing out cigarettes and all sorts of stuff to make some sort of a propaganda for themselves, I thought that I had to look for a place where I could make myself useful. And after a conversation with Captain Groen, I went to the north to see if there was anything I could do more on the location where the -- the most of the refugees were situated just south of the compound near the factory sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you in fact proceed up to that location, Major?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you describe to the Trial Chamber what you saw there.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: When I came up there, there was just a sort of a human chain of UN soldiers made to try to keep the refugees calm, and there was a lot of panicking and scared refugees present at that time there. And I took over -- basically, I took over from a colleague that was -- that was in charge there. But the situation was like I described before, chaotic, a lot of people were frightened, screaming and cramped together. And no one knew basically what would happen next.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At this time, I'd ask that 65 ter number 1516 be displayed, please. And can we actually flip that upside down? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd just ask you to take a moment and orient yourself to what's being displayed and ask you if you can identify what that depicts.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: In the centre of the picture I see the UN compound that was based in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And for the purposes of the way we positioned this, which direction is north, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: North is pointing up.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You described a factory area where you went to provide assistance to the other UNPROFOR soldiers and where you saw the refugees behind the human chain. I'd ask you if you can take -- there's a stylus to the right of the computer there. It's actually connected and Madam Usher will give you a hand with that. Now, I'd ask you to circle that factory area that you described on this map.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Not all of the area is on this map --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could maybe lift it up just a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Is that better, Major?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yeah, that's better. The general location or the whole area would be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I note that you've drawn a circle around a particular area that appears to bestride a road. And can you describe what road that is, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That is the road from the north, basically the only asphalted road in the enclave, going from north to south. From Bratunac to the down of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you also, while you're at it, please just indicate where the main DutchBat 3 compound itself was located.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So next to this so-called rectangle that you have just outlined, could you kindly put DC, the letters DC or Dutch compound.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And where you put the egg-shaped outline further down, could you describe it in your own words, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Refugee area. Okay. And could you just draw a small line along the road with -- that you indicated or you referred to before with an arrow pointing towards Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it has to be higher because I don't think it will show in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, I'm not an expert on this. Will it show on the record or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm not an expert either, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I would just ask that if maybe if you can draw the arrow inside that little egg shape and I think we will be safe.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it will be safer, yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And put an S just below the point, the arrow point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's it. And in between the two outlines could you just sign your name, please affix your signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's initials, but it's okay. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just looking at that -- this image, sir. Can you just describe approximately where your final blocking position was, just to give the Court an idea of how far you had to proceed to get there. If it's even on the map itself.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: My last location just north of 0.02, is just not on the map. It's just I think 400, 500 metres south of the last area I described as the refugee area and just north of the intersection 0.02.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: While you were working with the other UN soldiers at the factory area you described, did you see any high-level VRS officers arrive at that location?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I saw General Mladic making a visit to -- to the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how did you know it was Mladic, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Because I recognised him from things I had seen before on television, and of course from our training before we went to the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did you observe General Mladic doing while he was there?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Basically to me it was an extension of the thing -- the Serb soldiers -- the first Serb soldiers I had observed in the enclave also did was making more or less of a sort of a propaganda visit, handing out drinks or food to refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you meet any other VRS personnel who identified themselves as high-level?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The person from the VRS that identified himself as Mane, stating that he was a captain of a military police unit. He asked me if I was the high-ranking UN soldier in the area, so basically the commander there, outside of the compound of the UN. And he stated to me that he was the commander -- the local commander of the Serb forces there. And his name was Mane.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Was this Captain Mane accompanied by anyone?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Mane was accompanied by his interpreter Miki. Mane only spoke Serbo-Croatian, and Miki interpreted into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did Mane identify any particular unit he was with?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: He told me then that he was a military police unit and that he had some sort of liaison with the Drina Wolves, which at that time I thought was the Drina Corps. So Drina Wolves for me at that time was the same as the Drina Corps. And he stated to me that the military police unit had a liaison with the Drina Wolves but was not a part of the Drina Wolves.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at some point did you learn who this Captain Mane's commander was?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: At a certain stage he told me that his commander was code-named or nicknamed Stalin, and at several locations I also saw Stalin visiting the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did anyone give you a description of this Stalin before you actually saw Stalin?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Mane described him to me, and even when Stalin visited the area he pointed him out to me and stated that this man he had pointed out was Stalin.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you referred to code-name Stalin, what type of code are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: A code-name in the sense of when using the radio he used the name Stalin. That was the only name Mane told me about that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was the description that this Mane gave you of Stalin at the time?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Basically it was a very short description. A short person with a big pair of Ray-Ban sunglasses on, and together with him pointing that person out to me it was very clear that he meant that person.
