utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Anything else other than the Ray-Ban sunglasses that you remember?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Maybe he had told me at that time but I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: It was a very clear description of Stalin.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, at some point did you see someone who appeared to you to be Stalin's superior speaking with this Stalin?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: At some point I saw Stalin visiting the area, together with a well-known figure for us as Major Nikolic. Major Nikolic was a figure that was the whole period we were present there and even before our time was a well-known character. And I saw Major Nikolic together with Stalin, in which -- from which I drew the conclusion that Nikolic was the superior of Stalin. Nikolic more or less made some sort of an inspection visit with Stalin next to him. Nikolic walked in the centre of the road, Stalin alongside him, which seemed to me in gestures that he was explaining to Nikolic what was happening and what was going on and how they organised things. So that was the visit of Nikolic and Stalin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's specify which Nikolic this is. Referring to which Nikolic, Major Nikolic, do you know his first name by any chance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've heard his first name later on. At that time I only knew him as Major Nikolic, but later on I learned that it was Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Major, in addition to the VRS officers whom you've just described, do you recall meeting any other VRS officers during this period of time on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Like I told, there was a visit from General Mladic, and I also had a discussion with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you remember whether Mr. -- or General Mladic was accompanied by anyone during the visits with whom you had a conversation who may have identified himself as a logistics officer?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I don't know if that person identified himself to me as a logistics officer came together with General Mladic, but basically in the same period of time as General Mladic visited my location. After that, I also had a meeting with or came into contact with a person that said he was a colonel, and his name was Jankovic. And he told me that he was a logistics officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what language were you speaking with this colonel, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I spoke with him in English. He spoke excellent English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you describe what he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: He wore a uniform, a complete uniform together with a leather document brief-case more or less, bag.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was this Colonel Jankovic doing that you could see, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: It looked like he was more or less inspecting the area, looking around to see what -- what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that it's 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. We'll have a 30-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Major, when we broke you had just described meeting a series of Bosnian Serb officers. When we met some -- probably two weeks ago now, did I show you a series of photographs?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you identify various individuals in those photographs?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I recognised a few of the individuals, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honours, I'm going to be referring to various video stills which are contained in 65 ter 1936. It's a book of still images from the trial video, which I believe was distributed to Your Honours and to the Defence counsel as well. What we will be showing are a few of those stills except with the identifying information obviously cropped from the still, but I will identify each still by the chapter and page number that's contained on the document in case anybody wants to follow along with the -- with the actual document in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: For the record, sir, do you see an image before you?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes, now I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And for the record, this is chapter 16, page 5 of that book and there is an image of a man to the left of this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that person, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I recognise that person as being Mane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness is being shown a still image which bears ERN number 02164885. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we now see chapter 16, page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So I presume you recognise the person all the way to the right of that photograph.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That person is myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And for the record, this is chapter 16, page 6 of the photo stills book.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There is an individual in the centre of the picture, sir. Do you recognise that individual?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That person is Miki, and on the left side Mane again.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And Miki is the individual in the blue vest. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could be shown chapter 8, page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'd ask you whether you recognise anybody in this photograph; and if you do, if you would identify who you remember, moving from left in the image to right in the image, Major.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I recognise the person on the left wearing the sunglasses and the moustache as being Stalin. Then in the centre I recognise General Mladic, and on the right-hand side the two persons on the right-hand side, one wearing the sunglasses and a little bit left to him were the body-guards of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we'll speak about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. We need to -- so the photo or still image that the witness has been referred to is -- or bears ERN number 02164852. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And if we may be shown --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In my book it says chapter 10, page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I've been identifying it at the chapter and page number that's at the bottom of the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you said chapter 8 in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Oh, I apologise, it's chapter 10, page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Kwon. And thank you, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we may be shown chapter 8, page 4, which bears the ERN 0291-6181 in the top right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the individuals in this photograph, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I recognise on the left General Mladic and on the right a person I know as Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And finally if we may be shown chapter 9, page 1, which bears the ERN 0291-7813 at the top right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Major, do you recognise anyone in this photograph; and if so, would you identify them moving from left to right on the image?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: On the left-hand side I see the person that I know as Major Nikolic, then moving to right I see Colonel Jankovic. And right from him, the second person from the right, is one of the body-guards of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Major.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are four persons in the picture. You have -- you haven't told us whether you recognise the person at the extreme right of the picture.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The person on the extreme right, Your Honour, I don't recognise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to when you first met Captain Mane, Major. I believe you testified that he approached you and identified himself. Did he tell you why he was approaching you?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: He wanted to know if I was the local commander of the UN at that position or outside the compound, and he told me that the refugees were going to be transported out of the -- out of the enclave. And he wanted to know whether the UN would stay there or would go back to the compound; that was basically the choice he gave me when he was telling me that they were going to do the transports of the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you describe what Captain Mane's demeanour and tone of voice were when he told you that, sir.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: He was very clear and he brought it as a fact that the refugees were going to leave Srebrenica. He told me that 200 buses -- he mentioned the number of 200 -- were coming to pick up the refugees, and he brought it to me as a matter of fact. And he just wanted to know from me whether the UN would stay or would withdraw to the UN compound in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Major, based on what he said and the way he said it to you, what did you decide to do?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The fact that he also mentioned that the refugees were going to leave and that he wanted to know if the UN would stay, or otherwise the Serbs would do it their own way. The way he said it and the words he chose made me decide to stay there. Next to this, I thought it was one of our assignments to provide, if possible, humanitarian aid to the refugees. So I decided to stay there in the middle between the Muslim refugees and the Serb soldiers, instead of retreating to the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you just mentioned being in the middle of the refugees and the Serb soldiers. Do you mean that literally, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes, literally.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did the buses arrive?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes. Shortly after that - I don't know if it was the exact amount Mane mentioned - but there were a lot of buses but also trucks there, which indicated that what Mane had told me was a fact. Next to this, I was into contact with Major Franken, which was the second in command in our battalion, and he also stated that he -- he had heard something about the refugees being transported, so that made it clear to me that this really was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Of course we already were there in basically a human chain to try to keep the refugees calm, using interpreters to try to get them to sit down, to get out of the sun because the heat was -- was incredible, and people were collapsing from dehydration and the heat itself. So we literally stood in the middle and we try to keep the families together as they were let through to the -- to the transportation devices, buses and trucks and whatsoever. Basically the way it worked was that Mane told me how many buses or trucks that were present, so how many refugees could be seated in those trucks. And I would give orders to the UN soldiers to let people through, and letting them through in small groups so they would not trample each other and we could help those families to stay together and not getting hurt in another way because of the crowd that was -- that was tremendous.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, at that point, Major, were men and women being let through together?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: We always tried to keep families together and also when the amount of people was too big to be transported in the buses or trucks, we would also always make the division to keep families together so to keep a family at our location or let the whole family through. So we always let the men -- families together, so also the men together with their families. And at first this also was executed. Later on, I noticed that the men were singled out and they were no longer kept with their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you observe what, if anything, was being done with those men who were being singled out, Major?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The Serb soldiers behind my location singled out the Muslim men, and they were put to a lawn in front of houses without any facade. And they were put there to wait. They sat down on the lawn in front of the house, and of course I questioned Mane why they singled out the men from the women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what did Mane tell you, if anything, in response to your question?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Mane told me that they had a list of war criminal, Muslim war criminals, and that they were going to check if the persons, the men they singled out, were on the list of war criminals, which they wanted to try for their criminal actions earlier in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how did that explanation strike you at that time, Major?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Basically it was a clear explanation, and it is something armed forces do when they are in a conflict together and you make prisoners of war. And the explanation at that time was credible.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may be shown a clean copy of 65 ter 1516, please. And if we could just magnify it a little bit, as we did before, or a little less, please. Perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see an image before you?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again, can you describe just generally what this is for the Court.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The centre of the picture I see the UN compound, the base of Potocari, and of course the road alongside it from north to south.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, based on your knowledge of -- of that -- the compound and the area, is this aerial photograph a fair and accurate depiction of that location as you recall it?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, you've never -- have you ever flown over the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Based on your knowledge of the geography, sir, I'd ask if you could identify on this image the house that you described seeing some of the Muslim men being directed to on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I'd ask Madam Usher to assist Major Van Duijn in that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll try to circle the lawn in front of the houses. And in this area, this was the lawn where the -- the men were -- were gathered.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you would, just to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. So -- sorry to interrupt you like this, Mr. Thayer, I hate it. But -- Major, could you kindly write "lawn" next to -- next to that marking, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we are going to save it, he needs to sign it, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you would just place your initials or your signature --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought you hadn't finished with it, so that's why I didn't intervene with it before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it can be safely saved now, and I understand it will be tendered later on. Yes, go ahead, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Major, a moment ago you testified about the explanation you received from Captain Mane. Did you nevertheless intervene or protest with respect to certain separations that you observed?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The explanation from Captain Mane was that they wanted to search for war criminals; and although that was credible, I objected every time there was a clear view of the Serb soldiers singling out boys or old men that were too old or too young to be soldiers. So I objected with Mane when -- when the situation happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And on those occasions, Major, what would the result of your intervention be?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: On all the occasions I objected with Mane, he would let the -- the men go through and accompany the rest of their family to the buses. So at least at that position we had kept those boys or older men with their families together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer, again, sorry for interrupting you, but we had a problem with saving the image that the witness signed. Major, you need to sign it again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In whichever place you choose, and then it can be signed -- then it can be saved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think we can proceed, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Major, you described Captain Mane's role and his interaction with you, but who was actually conducting the separations and directing the refugees on to the various vehicles?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The Serb forces in the area. The UN soldiers never separated the men from the women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to your knowledge did the UN soldiers ever participate in actually placing people on the buses?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The only thing I remember and I recall is helping people to get on a truck, which I personally did myself as well. But just in a way to help people getting on to a truck or into the bus because they were not able to do that themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And from where you were located, sir, who was in command of those soldiers and that process?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: From my point of view, that was Mane.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Major, did you receive any reports from your men as to how the refugees were being treated as they boarded the buses?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Later on during the day I got reports that women and children and the people that wanted to board the buses were kicked or beaten by Serb soldiers to -- to get them into the buses, and that they were mistreated when they came near to the buses, which was a little bit more north of my location. So I could not see it myself, but I heard the report from soldiers that were there in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you observe any incidents yourself of that nature?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: On my location there were a few incidents where basically the area Mane and myself had agreed upon were crossed by Serb soldiers that entered in the middle of the area where only UN soldiers were. And one incident was very clear where a Serb soldier dressed in a black overall took hold of the throat of a young boy and tried to get him out of the -- of the group of people he was standing in waiting to get through to the buses. And at that point I intervened with Mane and convinced him that he had to get his personnel away from that area because that basically was what we agreed upon, that you had the group of Muslim refugees, then the UN soldiers, and behind myself the Serb soldiers, and not the Serb soldiers in the middle of the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how did the refugees react to being separated, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Of course this was a terrible course of events when you have families that want to be together and are placed in a position where nothing is certain. They were shelled at, they were fleeing from their homes. They only had some personal belongings with them which they could carry, and of course at the early stages the place where they would go was also uncertain. So this was a terrible situation when in that period of time also families were separated from each other, and men were being singled out by Serb forces and families literally tried to keep hold of each other and were forced by Serb soldiers to let go of each other and have the men separated and brought to that first location on the lawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, turning your attention, sir, to later that day, did General Mladic appear again?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you have an encounter with the General at that time?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: At first we had some sort of a general conversation in which he asked me if I was the commander on site, and we spoke about general things as soccer, football, the weather, and sports. And he wanted to know some things about the UN soldiers that were present at that location which were with me at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how was -- what language was this conversation being conducted in, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: General Mladic also had his interpreter with him, and I had an interpreter which was the dedicated interpreter of Bravo Company, but of course Bravo Company was not in place anymore. So this was a Muslim interpreter that helped me during that first day.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that General Mladic had some questions about your colleagues in DutchBat. Can you describe that conversation and any further detail for the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: There were a few DutchBat soldiers sitting alongside the road, and my conversation with General Mladic was just in front of them. And he asked me if I was from the Netherlands, and he also asked the soldiers if they were also from the Netherlands. And there was one Dutch soldier from apparently an African heritage with dark skin. And General Mladic asked me if he was also from the Netherlands or if he was from Ethiopia. And I explained to him that we had a multi-ethnic society in the Netherlands, multi-racial, and there were a lot of people looking different but they were all Dutch. And he answered to me that this was a big problem for the Netherlands and that in ten years from then the Serb army would be in the Netherlands protecting us from the Muslims and other races. And I told him I didn't believe him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Were the separations and transportation taking place in your area while this encounter with General Mladic was happening, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The whole process was still ongoing at that time, and General Mladic stayed a period of time. Not all of that period I was speaking to him, so he also was a period of time there without a conversation with me but just him being in the area and the process ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And while he was there, did you have to dispatch your interpreter to approach the General about something, Major?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes. At some point when I was no longer into a conversation with General Mladic but he was present, just about 50 to 100 metres behind my position, there was a problem in the group of refugees. And through my interpreter I heard that there was a mother totally hysterical and panicking because her five children had already been let through. And she had lost them in the -- in the chaos. And then it became clear to her because she saw her five children sitting in one of the last trucks that were already starting to leave the area, and she was still stuck in the group of refugees. When my interpreter made that clear, I took the decision to carry the woman fast, because she was a little bit weak, to the truck to get her to her five children. But at that time I had to cross basically the agreed line between the UN soldiers and the Serb soldiers behind us. I saw that General Mladic was present, and I was afraid that because of my action maybe one of the Serb soldiers would maybe even shoot me. So I knew that the one person present who could prevent that was General Mladic, so I sent my interpreter. I asked my interpreter to -- if he wanted to help me. And after he said yes, I asked him to go over to General Mladic, to run while I was running towards the trucks to explain to him that I was not doing something strange or radical or whatever, but that I was just bringing that woman to her children and that if he would make it clear to his soldiers that they would not shoot me. So I didn't look any further if this interpreter did that, and I went running. I brought the mother to her children, and when I came back I saw my interpreter standing near to General Mladic and I went over to them to see if -- and it was clear to me that the interpreter helped me and had done what I asked him to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you describe what happened next, Major.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The -- General Mladic made some sort of a sick role play with the interpreter in which he stated that General Mladic, himself, was a Muslim. He asked me if I knew the interpreter, and I confirmed of course. And I said: He's a good guy. He's a Serb, stating that my Muslim interpreter was a Serb and that General Mladic himself was a Muslim. And that he, as a Muslim - General Mladic I mean - was a bastard or other words -- I don't know what he used then. And he only thought about making babies, but that the interpreter -- and at that time also General Mladic took told of the interpreter and crushed him to his body, was a good guy, was a good fellow, because he was a Serb. But next to that, he also made clear that he didn't understand my actions but he was very mad about me sending the Muslim interpreter straight to General Mladic because it was not clear for him to he was interpreting for me. But he had a problem with the interpreter speaking directly to him. And he said that if that would happen again, he would shoot the interpreter personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Major, during this conversation who was actually doing the interpreting?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The Muslim interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was his reaction at the end of the conversation, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: He was incredibly scared, shivering, literally shivering all of his body. And he was actually so scared that I decided to get him back escorted -- let him be escorted back to the compound because he was not able to be there anymore. And he -- just to tell you how scared he was, he took hold of my back pocket, of the shorts I was wearing then, and he didn't want to let go of me and my back pocket until I brought him to a colleague that escorted him back to the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So how long did the separation and transport last on the 12th of July, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: It lasted until the evening, until it started to get dark. And then Captain Mane told me they would stop for the night, and the Serb forces would go back to Bratunac and celebrate in Hotel Fontana. And he told me to clear the road of people, the asphalted -- the only asphalted road leading from north to south, because they would need -- the Serb forces would need the road to transport troops to the south. And that the next day, on the 13th, they would start again with the transport at around 8.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did he also ask you for anything?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: He wanted me to hand over my pistol to him, which I didn't have anymore because at the starting of the day we had put the hand-guns in my APC. But he insisted and we even went over to my APC, but we discovered there that all the weapons were already gone from my APC and he was very disappointed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did he indicate to you whether he and his men would return the next day; and if so, did he give you a time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's just answered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Oh --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said clear: The way from north to south or from south to north, because my men will return on the 13th and start with the transport again at around 8.30 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I clearly missed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You had testified about the men sitting on the lawn in front of those two houses. Did you see what happened to them, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: In that process of ending -- basically ending the activities of the first day I saw that the men sitting on the lawn were transported by the Serbs using a truck that I raised as the truck that had earlier in the day had brought some bread and water, which I had requested through -- through Mane. And they were transported off from that lawn to a destination unknown.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall what direction they headed, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: They headed north.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where did you go after the separations and transportations ended that day?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: At first I briefed Lieutenant Koster who was taking over from me for the night. I asked him to make some sort of a V-shaped tunnel with our APCs that would make it easier for us the next day to keep hold of the refugees, to keep them more together which would need less personnel from us. So I asked him to re-arrange the APCs, and I left to go back to the compound to have a few hours of sleep because at that time I was very tired from the blocking positions and of course all the activities of the first day which had left for me in three, four days only a few hours of the sleep. So we agreed upon me getting back to the compound to have a few hours of sleep and then returning the next morning early.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And on your way back to the compound, sir, did you see anything in particular that you recall now?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: When I headed back, I saw a roll call of Serb forces. They were standing in a U-shaped formation, and I recognised at the head of that roll call the person I know as Stalin.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I won't show you that aerial photograph again, Major, but could you just describe for the Trial Chamber approximately where that roll call occurred.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: On the way from my location, so basically the houses with the lawn, towards the UN base on the left-hand side of the road. On the west side you have the white house, and just before that, so between the house with the lawn and the white house, they had the roll call on the middle of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall approximately how many Serb soldiers you saw in the roll call, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: If I have to make an estimation now, I would say somewhere around 50 to 70 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again, without trotting out that aerial photograph, sir, can you describe for the Trial Chamber approximately where the separations that you were observing took place. And if you care to refer to any of the landmarks you've already talked about, please do.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Basically the separations occurred in exactly the area where the roll call was, so between -- at the first day the house with the lawn and before the house on the lawn on the road. And the second day, a little bit more to the north on the location of the roll call just south of the white house.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. You've referred to a white house, sir. That is -- is that the same house that you were describing with the lawn in front of it or is that a different house?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: This is a different house closer to the UN compound just south of the UN compound but on the other side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll talk about that in a little while. So that brings us to the morning of 13 July. Did you return to that same area where you had been working until the previous night, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes. After, of course, briefing my commander when I came back the night before and a few hours sleep, I went back to the position of Lieutenant Koster which had taken over from me for the night, and I was there approximately 6.00 in the morning. So earlier than the -- Mane had stated the night before. And I took over from Koster again, and he explained to me that -- the things that had happened during the night. And I took over from him from that moment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just briefly, sir, without going into much detail, what did Lieutenant Koster tell you he had heard happened over the previous night?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: He basically explained what they had done, that they had been physically with the Muslim refugees, trying to keep them calm because every once in a while panic broke out, and that people were standing up and running towards the location, they thought something had happened. Other things that also happened was that people were injuring themselves, hitting themselves on the head with bricks or something else in order to -- in the hope that if they were injured or wounded, that they would get a better treatment and would be treated and transported to the Red Cross. So next to that self-inflicted wounds, there was also a man that had hung himself during the night in one of the -- in one of the factory sites. And UN personnel had to get him down off that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you and Lieutenant Koster had discussed placing the APCs in a particular position. Had that been done by the time you returned in the morning of the 13th, Major?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes, he had positioned the APCs that I requested to him, and they resembled some sort of a V-shape on the road, narrowing the road a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So what happened next, Major?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Next -- after I took over from Koster and he was still present there, we were both surprised that the -- the buses already entered the enclave and were already present, and the bus drivers were basically waiting for instructions. And at that time I decided to already start the transports in order to keep the families together and let the families and refugees enter the buses without being abused or kicked or whatever in -- in a normal fashion. So without the Serb forces, I started with the transportation because it was clear to me that the refugees could not stay there -- in fact, the refugees were even eager to leave the -- the place where they had been there, the factory sites because there was a big threat of epidemics starting to break out. People were sitting in their own excrements. People were injured, people were wounded, so there was no place for them without food, without water to stay, and it was clear that they really had to leave there quickly. So I decided to already start the transports.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did the Serb soldiers return that morning, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: As Mane had said before, the evening before, they returned at 8.30. They were even surprised that we already started the transports, but I was very happy to learn that the NIOD report that was made later on and was very detailed later took hold of Muslim men, refugees that in those precious one and a half, two hours were able to leave the enclave in the buses without being singled out by Serb soldiers. So I was very happy that I started that morning without the Serb soldiers being present.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So what happened when the Serb soldiers returned, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: When Mane and the Serb soldiers were present again from around 8.30, the men were being singled out again and the whole process, as the first day, was started up again with that -- with one distinction, that the men that were singled out were not brought to the house with the lawn - as I described earlier - but to the white house which was closer to the compound, just south of the compound, and a little bit more to the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, on this second day of separations and transportations, sir, who was conducting the separations and directing the refugees to the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The Serb forces and Mane leading them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at some point during that day, do you remember an incident involving a water truck?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Basically after the -- the big group of refugees was already gone, so there was no huge concentration of people anymore, so the task of the UN soldiers was becoming less. And we were just helping the sick and the wounded and helping them to either go to the Red Cross or to go to the buses. One of my soldiers came up and told me that the water truck that we had placed to -- near to the -- the place where we had the injured and the wounded people assembled to be treated by -- in any which way we could by our medical staff, that the Serb forces wanted to take away that water truck. That's when I decided to go over there to explain that the water truck was not for the UN, although it was a white UN-marked water truck, but that it was basically a water truck that was there for the sick and the wounded. And the Serb forces tried to -- tried to tow it away with a tractor.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, while you were dealing with this issue, sir, were you informed about a problem with this white house to which you had referred earlier in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: During that whole process of me protesting against taking away of the water truck, one of the UNMOs, Mr. Kingori, came up to me and he explained to me that there was a problem with the white house and that it was too crowded with -- with men that were singled out. And basically it was necessary to take a look there and to see what we could do to help the men that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we may at this time be shown a clean copy of 65 ter 1516, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see the image in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And with the assistance of Madam Usher, I'd ask you, given this level of magnification, can you identify where that white house that you testified about is located?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I think I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you please circle it and write "white house" next to it, please.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And place your initials next to that as well.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, Madam Registrar, we need to save it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we may be shown 65 ter 1535, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see an image on your screen, Major?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recognise what's depicted in the -- more or less the centre of the image?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: This is the house I know as the white house.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is there anything that's different about the surroundings in this photograph than when you were there, Major?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The biggest difference is that the vegetation was more thick and that the bushes around the -- basically the front lawn of the house were so thick that you couldn't -- or barely could see the house from the roadside on. So there was much more vegetation around the house and the front lawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: After the -- the UNMO had told you about this problem -- and by the way, do you remember the name of the UNMO?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and that's Kingori.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you go over to the white house after he told you about the problem?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what did you see there, if anything?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I saw a lot of men crammed as the UNMO Kingori had told me, crammed inside the house, and a few of them sitting just in front of the house. The whole house was basically packed with men, and in front of the house the whole front lawn, which is empty now on the screen, but was then packed with a mixture of personal belongings, photographs, and also, as I saw then, passports from the men that were sitting inside the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How did the men appear to you that you saw?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The men looked to me very scared and frightened, weakened, and very quiet, looking at -- looking -- also looking at me with -- with open eyes but very -- they appeared to me very scared and weakened.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you do anything with any of these documents or passports that you described, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I started assembling the passports because I thought maybe a few of the men had lost them, and I had both my pockets filled with -- with those passports. And I don't know why, but later on I put those passports out of my pockets and put them there again. But seeing those passports raised a question to me, which I also posed to Mane, that basically together with Miki had followed me from the first location, the water truck to the white house. And I posed a question to him, that if the explanation he had given me about the war criminals was correct, that the men would need their passports to prove their identity, to show that they were in fact not on the list of war criminals or differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did Captain Mane say to you in response to that?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Basically he -- he grinned at me and he told me that the men didn't need the passports anymore, which at that point made clear to me that there was a very dark future ahead for the men in the house - and in fact for the men that had been singled out the day before. At that stage, I thought about the images I had seen before -- before going on mission, images from 1991, 1991/1992 of the camps that were in Bosnia during the war. So I had visions of that in my mind, and I wanted to make sure that we would accompany the men that were being transported, the buses were already there, from the white house out of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So what steps did you take in that regard, sir?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I tried to get on the bus myself, but was forced at gunpoint -- and by Mane telling me not to do that because it was not going to happen very -- he was very deliberate -- very clear in that I was not going on the bus and that to him it was not worth it. So literally at gunpoint I had to stop my actions to get on the bus myself. And I radioed in to the battalion operations room, our battalion operations room, to make sure that we would accompany the buses with the men. And the response I got was that they would do everything in their power to get those buses escorted. Later on they -- I heard that they tried it, but somewhere it went wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I really don't want to interrupt my colleague, but I was just trying to make sure that everything that the witness said is properly recorded in the transcript. Because I don't believe that he said that actually Mane was gunpointing at him, but here we have on page 72, line 20: "I tried to get on the bus myself, but was forced at gunpoint and by Mane..." So I don't believe that he actually said that Mane pointed a gun on him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you are correct. I think that -- he first stated that he was forced at gunpoint to get down or not to get -- and then Mane told him -- if you could actually confirm this to us, Major. I heard you say so, so it's just more for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, you are right. I was forced at gunpoint, but not by Mane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Lazarevic, for pointing that out to us. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did Mane exercise any physical control over you at that time, Major?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Basically he pulled me from the position next to the bus where I was trying to enter the bus, and he pulled me from that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I want to turn your attention to a slightly different topic. At some point did you and Lieutenant Koster receive some information that caused him to go investigate?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes. At the morning of the 13th when I had taken over from him, we had some information by MSF, brought to us by MSF, that there were some bodies behind houses in the area, next to the area we were in. And she asked if we could take a look if that was true or not because she had received that information. And basically because I had taken over from Lieutenant Koster, we agreed upon that he would go to there to basically inspect if the information MSF had was true or false.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at some point later, did you see Lieutenant Koster again?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Later on I saw Lieutenant Koster again, and he was very agitated and said to me that he couldn't explain everything but that he needed to get back to the compound of DutchBat and that he was afraid that they - the Serb soldiers he meant - were searching for him. And because I already knew Lieutenant Koster for a few years before that, I saw from his facial expression that he was -- he was very serious and that there was something very serious going on for him to react like that. And later I had heard that he had found some bodies behind a house.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately what time on 13 July the transportations ended?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Basically, as I think back now, it must have been around -- somewhere around 5.00 or 6.00 in the afternoon, so the late afternoon of the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you describe for the Trial Chamber what the Potocari compound and the factory areas looked like after the transportations were completed on that day.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: The factory areas were totally empty, and a lot of personal items were abandoned at that location. Basically it was a mess with all sorts of personal items going from photographs to blankets to pieces of personal interest that people wanted to take with them. And basically, those factory areas were totally -- totally desolate. And the Potocari compound was also empty, but there were still a few refugees there which were wounded with the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to show you a video film clip. It is from 65 ter 2047. And -- I'm sorry P02047. And the start time, I believe, is 1 minute -- I'm sorry, 1 hour, 58 minutes, and 5 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have an image in front of you on your screen?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and we are at 1 hour, 58 minutes, point 11, point 4 second.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see an individual at the far right hand of the screen in a blue vest and blue helmet?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That's the UNMO I know as Kingori.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Please continue. [Videotape played].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the individual at the far right of the screen -- And for the record we are at 1 hour, 58 minutes, 43.5 seconds.

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: I recognise him as being Lieutenant Koster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why would it be the far right?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sorry, the far left. It's been a long day, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again, on the far right of the screen at 1 hour, 58 minutes, 51.5 seconds, again do you recognise the individual in the sunglasses?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That's the person I know as Stalin.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. I think we'll go to another clip or further along in the video to 2 hours, 25 minutes, and 40 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just pause there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, 2 hours, 26 minutes, 13 seconds point 1, this -- I believe you've seen a similar image before, but who is the individual in the centre?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That's the person I know as Miki.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And on the left?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: That's the person I know as Mane.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is being discussed at this point, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: No, I don't recall what -- what the discussion was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's continue then, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And for the record at 2 hours, 27 minutes, 10.9 seconds, can you describe what is going on here at this point in the video?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Here my soldiers explained to me that the Serb forces, by using the tractor that's in front of the water truck, the water truck is the white truck with "UN" on the side, that they want to tow away the water truck. And MSF had explained to me that they still needed the water truck for the injured and sick people that were still on a location just to the right. We gathered them there to help them before transporting them to the compound or to another place. [Videotape played].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Could we just pause it there. Just a little ways back.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, the individual who is depicted at the left-most part of the screen at 2 hours, 28 minutes, 24.2 seconds in the camouflage shirt, do you recognise who that is?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: No, I don't recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, can you describe what that conversation with UNMO Kingori was about?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: At that stage Kingori explained to me, like you see in the film, that we had to shift our attention to the men in the white house, which basically at that point was possible for us because the big group of refugees had already left. And after one of my soldiers, who was an expert in transportation, made sure that the brakes were put on the water truck in such a way that it was not able for the Serb tractor to take the water truck away. And MSF had told me that they already had sped up the process to take away the wounded and sick from that location back to the compound. There was room for us to shift our attention to the men being cramped together in the white house.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the conversation that we just saw at the very end of the clip with UNMO Kingori, was it after that that you then went to investigate the white house?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: Yes. Directly after that I went with Kingori and also Miki and Mane trailing me towards the white house.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, during those two days of separations and transportations, was there any separation in particular that stays out or stands out in your mind more than others?

utterances.speaker: LEENDERT CORNELIS VAN DUIJN
utterances.text: There are still all the separations and the whole process was terrible, and still I think back at those situations. And of course, when you have a family that consists of more than five, six people and you are standing in the middle of the process in which the man is being separated from his wife and family and you literally -- they literally take you by the arm to -- to help -- ask if you can help or if you can aid in any way, then this is something that burns into your soul, especially when, in that specific incident, there is the classic boarder case in which you have a man that is old but not that old. He could be -- could have been a soldier for the Muslim forces, and especially because in that specific incident I decided not to protest with Mane. So the separation happened and the man was separated from his family. And that together with other decisions I had to take, in the cases where you don't protest, that is something that will stick with me the rest of my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Major, I have no further questions. Thank you. Your Honour, I see that it's approaching 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Major, we are going to stop here for the day. We'll continue tomorrow in the afternoon, starting with the first cross- examination. I -- have you changed the roster? You're sticking to the same -- all right. Okay. So it will be the Defence -- Defence for Mr. Popovic that will go first. We'll start at 2.15 tomorrow, and we hopefully will try to finish on Friday. Let's -- that's the effort that we will be collectively making. Thank you. Have a nice evening. See you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 28th day of September, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.
